notes.h: Cell — The Basic Unit of Life
items: Every living thing is made of cells. The cell is the basic level at which life exists; in multicellular organisms cells form tissues, organs and organ systems, yet each cell stays the basic unit of structure and function.

The human eye cannot separate two points closer than 0.1 mm, so most cells are invisible to it. Lenses in a light microscope magnify cells; an electron microscope uses a beam of electrons to show details at the nanometre scale.

notes.h: Estimating the Size of a Cell
items: Measure the field of view with a mm ruler, change it to micrometres, and divide by the number of cells across it; total magnification = eyepiece power × objective power.

notes.h: Cell Membrane — Structure and Selective Permeability
items: Every cell is enclosed by a very thin cell membrane (7–10 nm) of lipids and proteins. It is selectively permeable, and its structure is explained by the fluid-mosaic model.

notes.h: Osmosis — Movement of Water Across the Membrane
items: Water moves across a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute solution (more water, less solute) to a concentrated one until both are equal — osmosis. A cell swells in a hypotonic solution, stays the same in an isotonic one and shrinks in a hypertonic one.

notes.h: Cell Wall — The Outer Covering of Cells
items: Plant, fungal and bacterial cells have a rigid but permeable cell wall outside the membrane. It keeps plant cells firm in shape; animal cells have no wall and can change shape.

Inside the membrane is jelly-like cytoplasm with organelles and the nucleus. The nucleus has a double membrane with pores and a nucleolus; its DNA, as chromatin, becomes chromosomes before division, and genes in DNA carry the instructions that control the cell.

notes.h: Ribosomes, ER and Golgi — Making and Packing
items: Ribosomes make proteins; the ER (rough with ribosomes, smooth without) makes and carries proteins, fats and some hormones; the Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packs them into vesicles for transport, secretion or lysosome formation.
Lysosomes are single-membrane sacs filled with enzymes that break down unwanted proteins, carbohydrates, fats and even damaged cell parts; the products are released into the cytoplasm and reused.

A mature plant cell usually has one large central vacuole filled with cell sap; it stores water, minerals, sugars and wastes, and its water pressure keeps the cell firm. When it loses water the plant wilts. Animal cells have small, temporary vacuoles, if any.

notes.h: Mitochondria — The Powerhouse of the Cell
items: Mitochondria have two membranes; the inner one is folded into cristae that increase the surface area. Glucose is broken down here in cellular respiration, and the energy is stored as ATP, the energy currency of the cell.
Mitochondria have their own DNA and ribosomes and make some of their own proteins.
No mitochondria → no ATP from respiration → most cell activities stop.

Plastids make and store food in plant cells. Chloroplasts (with green chlorophyll in disc-shaped membranes in the stroma) carry out photosynthesis; chromoplasts hold yellow, orange or red pigments; colourless leucoplasts store starch, oils or proteins.
Mitochondria and plastids have their own DNA and ribosomes, so they share an evolutionary history with bacteria-like single-celled organisms.

Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no well-defined nucleus — their DNA lies in a nucleoid — and no membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotic cells (plants, animals) have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; plant cells add a wall, plastids and a large vacuole.

New cells are formed only from pre-existing cells by cell division, which lets organisms grow, repair and reproduce. Mitosis gives two genetically identical daughter cells with the same DNA and chromosome number as the parent.

notes.h: Meiosis and Errors in Cell Division
items: Meiosis happens only in reproductive organs: the parent cell divides twice to form four gametes with half the chromosomes, so fertilisation restores the number and offspring vary. Errors in mitosis can cause tumours; errors in meiosis can cause genetic disorders.

notes.h: Life Span of a Cell — Contact Inhibition and Cancer
items: Every cell has a definite life span: it grows and divides in a controlled way, works and dies when no longer needed. Contact inhibition stops many animal cells from dividing when they touch neighbours; cancer cells lose this control and form tumours.

Schleiden (all plants, 1838), Schwann (all animals, 1839) and Virchow (new cells only from pre-existing cells, 1855) gave the cell theory: all organisms are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of structure and function, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells.
The cell theory unifies all biology, from bacteria to humans.
It explains the continuity of life through cell division.
Tiny cells make energy, make and secrete substances, divide and work together — you are a product of them.

items: In a multicellular organism, similar cells group into tissues, tissues into organs, organs into organ systems and systems into the organism; each tissue does one job, so the body works efficiently (division of labour).
Life begins as one cell dividing many times; the cells form skin (protection), muscles (movement), bones (support) and nerves (control and coordination).

notes.h: Why are Plant and Animal Tissues Different?
items: Plants stay fixed and make their own food; animals move and eat food. So their tissues differ in support, flexibility, nutrition, transport and growth.
Plants grow in length only at the tips of roots and shoots, where actively dividing cells (apical meristem) are found.
Stems of dicot plants grow thicker because a ring of actively dividing cells in the stem (lateral meristem) makes new cells inside and outside; yearly growth shows as annual rings.
Intercalary meristem at the base of internodes (just above nodes) lets plants like grasses grow again after cutting or grazing.
Meristematic cells are built for fast division; some of their daughter cells lose the ability to divide and become specialised permanent tissues — this is differentiation.
The epidermis is the outermost single layer of tightly packed cells, covered by a waxy cuticle, that protects the plant; root hairs absorb and stomata allow gas exchange and transpiration.
Protects against mechanical injury, water loss, harmful microorganisms and extreme conditions.
Parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma are simple permanent (supporting) tissues; their wall thickness decides whether they store, bend or stay hard.

notes.h: Complex Permanent Tissues — Xylem and Phloem
items: Xylem and phloem are complex permanent tissues — several kinds of cells working together; xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots, phloem carries food from the leaves.
Plant tissues work in three tissue systems — dermal (outer cover), ground (main body) and vascular (xylem and phloem); one tissue can carry several labels.
Epithelial tissue covers the body and lines internal organs with closely packed cells; its shape (thin, layered, tall, gland or receptor cells) matches its job.
Closely packed cells keep out germs, reduce water loss, and help absorption, secretion and movement of substances.
Connective tissue connects and supports other tissues; the kind depends on its matrix — watery in blood, hard in bone, jelly-like in cartilage — while tendons and ligaments tie the skeleton together.
Skeletal muscle gives voluntary movement; smooth and cardiac muscle give involuntary movement; their cell shape, nuclei and striations differ.
Nervous tissue, made of neurons, receives, processes and passes messages; the brain is the control centre and muscles act on its instructions.
Bones, muscles, joints, cartilage, tendons and ligaments form the musculoskeletal system; under nervous control, muscles pull bones through tendons and the bones move at joints.
The shape of the bone ends at a joint decides the movement: ball and socket (all directions), hinge (one direction), pivot (turning), fixed (none).
The skeleton — skull, vertebral column and rib cage — gives strength and protects organs; cartilage makes the spine and rib cage flexible enough to bend and to breathe.
Some mature plant cells can undo their specialisation, divide and redifferentiate into a whole plant (totipotency); this is the basis of plant tissue culture and crop improvement.

notes.h: Position, Reference Point, Rest and Motion
items: The position of an object is its distance AND direction from a fixed reference point at an instant. If the position changes with time the object is in motion; if not, it is at rest — so rest and motion depend on the reference point.
Fix a reference point first; position = distance + direction from it
Motion = position changing with time; rest = position not changing
Rest and motion are always 'with respect to' a reference point

Distance travelled is the total length of the path (numerical value only); displacement is the net change in position — its magnitude is the distance between the start and end positions and it has a direction. Both are in metres; |displacement| ≤ distance.
For straight-line motion, distance travelled = magnitude of displacement only if the object moves in one direction without turning back
Ball rolling down a straight incline (Fig 4.6): distances 40, 50, 70, 100 cm at A, B, C, D = magnitudes of displacement

Average speed = total distance ÷ time interval (no direction); average velocity = displacement ÷ time interval (with direction). Both in m s⁻¹; they are equal in size only when the object moves in one direction.
Average speed = magnitude of average velocity when the object moves in one direction (no turning back)
Speedometer reading ≈ magnitude of the velocity at an instant; the direction of the tyres gives its direction
In this chapter 'velocity' means velocity at an instant

Average acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time interval, a = (v − u)/(t₂ − t₁), in m s⁻². It points along the velocity when the object speeds up and opposite to it when it slows down; it can also come from a change in direction.
A sudden start or stop of a vehicle gives a jolt — we feel the change in velocity
An object can move very fast and yet have zero acceleration (bus at constant high velocity on a straight road)
Acceleration can come from a change in magnitude of velocity, its direction, or both

notes.h: How to Plot a Position-Time Graph
items: A graph shows how one quantity (position) depends on another (time): draw axes, choose a scale, plot each pair as a point and join the points — uniform motion gives a straight line, speeding up gives a curve.
A graph is not a route map — it shows how position changes with time, not the path
Points between the plotted ones are correct for a vehicle moving at constant speed
Graphs in this chapter are for straight-line motion in one direction: distance = |displacement|, speed = |velocity|
Graphs help compare two motions, calculate quantities and see whether motion is uniform

The shape of a position-time graph shows the kind of motion (straight sloping line = constant velocity, curve = changing velocity, flat line = rest) and its slope gives the velocity: v = (s₂ − s₁)/(t₂ − t₁).
Steeper line = higher velocity

notes.h: Work Done by a Constant Force
items: Work done on an object by a constant force = force × displacement in the direction of the force (W = F × s). Its SI unit is the joule.

items.text: Always say WHICH force (agency) does the work and ON WHICH object.

items: The sign of work depends on the directions of force and displacement: same direction → positive, opposite → negative; no force, no displacement, or force perpendicular to displacement → zero.
An object that has the capacity to do work has energy. Work done on an object appears as a change in its energy: work done = change in energy.

items.text: Positive work on an object → it gains energy; it can then do work on another object and transfer that energy.

items: Energy exists in many forms — mechanical, thermal, light, sound, electrical, nuclear, chemical — and can change from one form to another.
Name the form BEFORE and AFTER for any device or process: from → to.

Positive work → velocity and KE increase; negative work → they decrease; no work → KE stays constant.
KE ∝ v²: double the speed → 4 times the KE; KE ∝ m: double the mass → 2 times the KE.
Potential energy is energy stored in an object because of its deformation (shape), or in a system of objects because of their relative positions.

items.text: An external force must overcome the internal forces to deform an object; when it is removed, the internal forces undo the deformation and can do work — so internal forces allow energy to be stored.

items: A motionless stretched rubber band has potential energy but no kinetic energy.
Raising an object of mass m by height h near the Earth needs work mgh; this is stored as gravitational potential energy U = mgh of the Earth–object system (called the PE of the object).

items.text: U = mgh is valid only near the Earth's surface; far away g decreases (Next Level Up).
Work done against gravitational, electric or magnetic forces can be stored as PE — but work done against friction is not stored.

items: Moving horizontally at constant velocity does not change PE; raising the object increases it.

items.text: In nature energy has many forms; the total energy of a system with no external forces stays constant.

items: At the highest point of a ball thrown straight up: KE = 0, PE is maximum; gravity still acts, so force ≠ 0 and acceleration = g (not zero).

items.text: Energy conservation can give final speed or position without working through the detailed motion — often simpler than Newton's laws.

items: Power is the rate at which work is done: P = W/t. SI unit watt (1 W = 1 J s⁻¹).

notes.h: Simple Machines: Effort, Load and Mechanical Advantage
items: Simple machines make a task easier by changing the size or direction of the force we apply; they never reduce the total work. Mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort.

items.text: Many machines are made of two or more simple machines; in all of them the work we put in = useful work on the load (ignoring friction). Machines do not create energy.

items: Real machines slow down and stop because friction (and air resistance) turn some energy into heat — so a perpetual motion machine cannot work.

Energy to raise a flag depends on its weight (mass, g) and the height; a fixed pulley does not change the work.
An inclined plane lets us raise a load with a smaller force applied over a longer distance: F′ × L = mgh, so MA = L/h (greater than 1).

items.text: Work done is the same in every case: if the force decreases, the displacement increases.

items: A lever is a rigid bar that turns about a fixed point (fulcrum). It balances when effort × effort arm = load × load arm, so MA = effort arm ÷ load arm.

items.text: A lever reduces the force but not the total work: the effort end moves a larger distance.

notes.h: Early Ideas of the Atom and Dalton's Theory
items: Over 2,000 years ago thinkers in India and Greece imagined matter divides down to smallest indivisible particles (parmanu, atomos); in 1808 Dalton turned the idea into a scientific theory based on experiments.
Kanada → parmanu; Democritus → atomos; Dalton (1808) → first scientific atomic theory
After Dalton the questions were: what are atoms made of, what do they look like, what makes atoms of different elements different?

notes.h: Discovery of the Electron and Thomson's Model
items: Radioactivity and Thomson's cathode rays showed atoms contain tiny negative electrons; since atoms are neutral, Thomson pictured a sphere of positive charge with electrons spread through it (plum pudding).
Electron = first subatomic particle found (Thomson, Nobel 1906)
Thomson's model was the first real attempt to show how + and − charges stay balanced

notes.h: Gold Foil Experiment and Rutherford's Model
items: α-particles fired at thin gold foil mostly passed straight through, some deflected and a few bounced back — so the atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus (protons) and electrons revolving around it.
Most pass → empty space; few bounce → tiny dense + nucleus
Protons carry the nucleus's positive charge; number of protons = number of electrons in every atom

Rutherford's revolving electron should lose energy and spiral into the nucleus, but atoms are stable; Bohr (1913) proposed electrons move only in fixed shells (K, L, M, N) of definite energy, where they lose no energy.
Limitation of Rutherford = stability; Bohr's fix = stationary states
Later the quantum mechanical model replaced fixed paths with electron clouds (higher grades)

notes.h: Discovery of the Neutron and the Three Subatomic Particles
items: Helium has twice hydrogen's protons but about four times its mass, so something neutral adds mass: Chadwick's neutron (1932). The atom's mass is mainly protons + neutrons in the nucleus; electrons, protons and neutrons are its three subatomic particles.
Atom's mass ≈ protons + neutrons
Atoms are heavier than their protons alone because of neutrons
118 elements known today; 69 were known by 1869
Element symbols went from Dalton's pictures (1803) to Berzelius's letters from Latin names (1813); today IUPAC approves names and symbols so scientists everywhere understand each other.
One shared set of symbols removes language barriers — different symbols would cause confusion and mistakes
Atomic number Z = number of protons (= electrons in a neutral atom) and fixes the element; mass number A = protons + neutrons (nucleons). From any two of Z, A, p, n, e we can find the rest.
Different Z → different element; Z is the element's identity card
A − Z = neutrons

Electrons fill shells from the nucleus outward by the Bohr–Bury rules: shell n holds at most 2n² (K 2, L 8, M 18) and the outermost shell at most 8; the distribution (e.g. Na 2, 8, 1) is the electronic configuration.
Write the config by subtracting down: 2 for K, then up to 8 for L, the rest in M (stop early when nothing is left)
Total of the config = Z

Atoms with an octet (He: 2) in the valence shell are stable; others lose, gain or share electrons to complete it. Valency = the number of electrons lost, gained or shared — the atom's combining capacity.
≤ 4 valence electrons: lose them (valency = v); > 4: gain (valency = 8 − v); 4: share
Valency = combining capacity

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers (different neutrons). Same electrons → same chemical properties; different masses → different physical properties. Some isotopes are useful in energy, medicine and dating.
Isotopes differ only in neutrons
Chemistry depends on valence electrons, not on neutrons
An element is a mix of isotopes in fixed proportions, so its atomic mass is the weighted average: each isotope's mass × its % abundance ÷ 100, added up (Cl = 35.5 u), not the simple average.
The average lies closer to the more abundant isotope
Quick check: answer must be between the smallest and largest isotope mass
Isobars are atoms of different elements with the same mass number but different atomic numbers (⁴⁰Ca, ⁴⁰K, ⁴⁰Ar) — the opposite pattern to isotopes.
isoTOPEs: same place (same element, same Z) · isoBARs: same 'weight' number (same A)
The atom's story is not over: electron clouds, and microscopes (STM, TEM) now image atoms

Wrong: If an atom has electrons, it must be negatively charged. Right: The positive charge equals the total negative charge, so the atom is neutral
Wrong: The gold foil experiment proved neutrons exist. Right: It showed a nucleus; neutrons were found by Chadwick in 1932
Wrong: Electrons can be anywhere around the nucleus with any energy. Right: In Bohr's model they move only in allowed shells with fixed energy
Wrong: Every nucleus has neutrons. Right: Ordinary hydrogen (protium) has no neutron
Wrong: Writing CO and Co means the same. Right: Co is cobalt; CO (two capitals) means carbon and oxygen together — the second letter must be small

Water does not burn or help burning, unlike hydrogen and oxygen, yet the mass of water formed = mass of hydrogen + mass of oxygen
Weigh in a closed system whenever a gas is formed
In any compound the elements are always combined in a fixed ratio by mass, whatever the source or method of preparation (Proust). Purified water from anywhere has hydrogen : oxygen = 1 : 8.
Ratio by MASS, not by number of atoms (water 1 : 8 by mass)

John Dalton (1808) explained both laws: matter is made of indivisible atoms that only rearrange in a reaction; atoms of an element are identical; they combine in simple whole-number ratios, and a compound always has the same number and kinds of atoms.
The two laws formed the basis of Dalton's theory; in a reaction atoms merely rearrange

Atoms with fewer than 8 valence electrons (2 for the K-shell) share, gain or lose electrons to become stable; this lowers the energy. The force that holds the atoms together is a chemical bond, and joined atoms can form molecules of elements or compounds.
When atoms combine, the total energy becomes lower than that of the separate atoms, so the arrangement is more stable
Neon (2, 8) and helium (2) already have full shells — they neither share nor transfer

A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons that attracts both nuclei. One shared pair = single bond (H—H, Cl—Cl, H—Cl); two shared pairs = double bond (O=O). Sharing forms molecules of elements and of compounds.
Bonds an atom forms by sharing = electrons it needs: H 1, Cl 1, O 2, N 3, C 4

An atom with fewer than 4 valence electrons generally gives them away and becomes a positive cation; an atom with more than 4 valence electrons usually gains or shares electrons; when it gains, it becomes a negative anion. The electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions is the ionic bond; the ions build a 3-D crystal.
Charge of an ion = protons − electrons
Metals usually form cations; non-metals usually form anions

notes.h: Properties of Ionic and Covalent Compounds
items: Ionic compounds generally dissolve in water (not in kerosene or petrol), conduct electricity only when their ions are free to move (dissolved or molten), and have high melting and boiling points. Covalent compounds mostly do not dissolve in water but dissolve in kerosene and petrol, do not conduct, and usually have low melting and boiling points.
To conduct, a substance needs charged particles that are free to move

A covalent compound's name counts its atoms with prefixes (mono 1, di 2, tri 3, tetra 4, penta 5, hexa 6); the first element keeps its name, the second ends in -ide; mono- is dropped for the first element; drop the a/o of a prefix before a vowel.
mono- is used for the second element (carbon monoxide) but dropped for the first
Keep the 'i' of di/tri: dioxide, trioxide

Write the cation's name first, then the anion's; simple anions end in -ide. Metals usually form cations and non-metals anions. Some ions contain two or more atoms — polyatomic ions — and their names generally do not end in -ide. Table 9.1 lists the names, formulae and valencies of common ions.
Ammonium NH₄⁺ is a polyatomic CATION — it takes the first place in a name (ammonium chloride)
To write a covalent formula: write the symbols, write their valencies, cross the valencies over as subscripts (a 1 is not written). A covalent name with prefixes gives the formula directly.
Valency = combining capacity — electrons an atom shares (bonds it forms): H 1, Cl 1, O 2, S 2, N 3, C 4 (added)

Write the cation first and the anion second, put the charge numbers under them, cross them over, then divide by any common factor; use brackets when there are two or more polyatomic ions. The charges are not written in the final formula, and total positive charge = total negative charge.

No bracket for a single polyatomic ion: CaCO₃, not Ca(CO₃)

The molecular mass of a covalent compound is the sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms in one molecule (in u). Ionic compounds form crystals, not molecules, so they get a formula unit mass instead.
Unit: u (atomic mass unit)
In an ionic compound the simplest whole-number ratio of ions is a formula unit; its mass — the sum of the atomic masses of all its atoms — is the formula unit mass.

items: Sound is produced by vibrations — the periodic to and fro motion of an object. When the vibration stops, the sound stops.
Sound is produced by vibrating objects.
Strings, membranes, air columns, metal objects and vocal cords can all vibrate to make sound.
Sound travels through solids, liquids and gases (a medium), but not through vacuum.
Medium can be solid, liquid or gas.
No medium (vacuum) → no sound.

A sound wave is a series of alternating compressions and rarefactions travelling through a medium; the particles only vibrate about their mean positions, parallel to the direction of travel — a longitudinal, mechanical wave.
Sound wave = alternating C and R.
Particles vibrate parallel to travel → longitudinal.
Needs a medium → mechanical.
A sound wave transfers energy, not particles: the vibrating source passes energy to the medium through particle vibrations and collisions.
Sound is a form of energy.
Energy travels; particles do not.

notes.h: Graphical Representation of a Sound Wave
items: At an instant, the density of the medium rises above and falls below the average periodically with distance; plotted, it gives a wave-shaped curve whose highest point (crest) is a compression and lowest point (trough) a rarefaction.
Compression ↔ crest; rarefaction ↔ trough.
Dashed line = average density.

Wavelength (λ, m) is the distance between two consecutive crests or troughs; frequency (ν, Hz) is the number of density oscillations at a point per second; time period (T, s) is the time for one oscillation; ν = 1/T.
λ in m, ν in Hz, T in s.

Amplitude is the maximum change in density from the average; a larger amplitude carries more energy. Intensity is the sound energy passing through unit area perpendicular to the direction of propagation in unit time, and it falls as sound spreads away from the source.
Bigger amplitude → more energy.
Intensity falls with distance.
Speed of sound is the distance a crest travels per unit time; v = λ/T = λ × ν. It depends on the medium (solid > liquid > gas) and, in air, rises with temperature and humidity.
v = λν.
Solid > liquid > gas.
Warmer, more humid air → faster sound.
Pitch is how we perceive frequency: high frequency sounds shrill, low frequency sounds deep. Humans hear only 20 Hz – 20 kHz; below that is infrasonic, above it ultrasonic.
Frequency → pitch.
20 Hz – 20 kHz audible; below infrasonic, above ultrasonic.
Loudness is how we perceive amplitude: larger amplitude sounds louder, and loudness falls with distance. Intensity is measurable; loudness depends on the listener. Loud sound for long harms hearing.
Amplitude → loudness (dB).
Noise = unwanted / harmful sound.

Sound reflects from hard surfaces by the same laws as light. An echo is heard only if the reflected sound arrives at least 0.1 s after the original — so the reflecting surface must be at least 17 m away (v = 340 m s⁻¹). Distance = v × t ÷ 2.
0.1 s rule → 17 m minimum.
d = vt/2.

In a large hall, many reflections arriving less than 0.05 s apart make a sound persist after the source stops — reverberation. Halls are designed with soft, porous surfaces to keep it at a desirable level.
Multiple reflections, gaps < 0.05 s.
Reduced by soft, porous surfaces.

items: Sound beyond our hearing is very useful: infrasound detects earthquakes, eruptions and storms; ultrasound images organs, breaks kidney stones, welds, cleans, finds defects and locates objects by reflection — echolocation in bats and SONAR in ships.
Infrasound: natural events.
Ultrasound: medicine, industry, locating.
Sonar depth = v × t ÷ 2.

Fungi such as bread mould reproduce asexually by spores — tiny, light, usually single-celled bodies made in huge numbers in a sac or on a swollen vesicle; they float in air and germinate when they land on moist, warm food.
Spores need warmth and moisture (and food) to germinate.

In all asexual methods the central process is mitosis: a cell divides into two daughter cells, each with the same number of chromosomes, identical to the parent — so the offspring are clones; it is fast and increases numbers quickly in good conditions.
Asexual reproduction is fast and helps organisms increase their population quickly when conditions are favourable.

Sexual reproduction joins gametes from two parents; to stop the chromosome number doubling every generation, gametes are made by meiosis (diploid → haploid, one chromosome from each pair); random mixing of chromosomes makes every gamete — and every child — different, and this variation helps species survive and evolve.
Every human gamete has 23 chromosomes; when two gametes join, the zygote has 46 again.
Variation helps some individuals adapt to changing environments; over time this contributes to evolution.

The flower is the reproductive organ of flowering plants (angiosperms); a complete flower has four parts — sepals, petals, stamens (male: filament + anther with pollen) and pistil (female: stigma, style, ovary with ovules, each with an egg).
Colour and fragrance of flowers help reproduction — they attract pollinators.

Pollination — the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma — is necessary for fruit formation; it is self-pollination when the pollen comes from the same flower or another flower of the same plant, and cross-pollination when it comes from a flower of another plant of the same kind.
Without pollination there is no fruit or seed.
If a plant could only self-pollinate for many generations, there would be little mixing, so genetic diversity would fall and the plants would adapt less well.

Pollination depends on pollinators — wind, water, insects, birds — and flowers have features to match; wind-pollinated plants release huge numbers of light pollen grains for few seeds, while insect-pollinated plants make fewer, sticky pollen grains and form many more seeds per grain.

On a compatible stigma the pollen grain grows a pollen tube down the style into the ovary; the male gamete fuses with the egg in the ovule (fertilisation) to form a zygote that becomes an embryo; the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary the fruit; seeds disperse and germinate, and the variation from sexual reproduction is used in plant breeding.

Animals reproduce asexually and/or sexually; in sexual reproduction fertilisation is external (outside the body, in water — frogs, most fish) or internal (inside the female — reptiles, birds, mammals); external fertilisers lay many eggs because many are lost, while internal fertilisation protects the fertilised egg or embryo better.

notes.h: How Young Ones Develop and Survive
items: Every animal must make its gametes meet and keep its young alive long enough to grow; fish, amphibians and insects lay hundreds to thousands of eggs with little yolk that hatch into a feeding larva which later changes into the adult; reptiles and birds lay few yolk-rich eggs; mammals grow the zygote inside the mother and feed the young on milk.
Whether the young can find their own food at birth or need long feeding and care depends on how long the embryo develops inside the egg or the mother's body.

At puberty the reproductive organs mature and start producing gametes; in males the testes (in the scrotum, kept slightly cooler) make sperm and a hormone; sperm travel through the vas deferens to the urethra; the seminal vesicles and prostate add fluids that nourish the sperm and help them move.

Reproductive maturity: as a child grows into an adult the reproductive organs mature and begin producing gametes; a sperm and egg meeting inside the female form a zygote → embryo → foetus in the uterus.

The female reproductive system has a pair of ovaries (make eggs and hormones), oviducts (fallopian tubes) joining each ovary to the uterus, the uterus (a bag-like organ where the foetus develops) and the vagina, joined to the uterus by the narrow cervix.
The hormones from the ovaries bring about the changes in girls during puberty.

Gametogenesis — the formation of gametes in the testes and ovaries — happens by meiosis, which halves 46 chromosomes to 23 so that the zygote has 46 again; males make numerous tiny motile sperm, females a single large egg; the father's sperm (X or Y) decides the baby's biological sex.
This difference between sperm and egg in size, number and structure is seen across most animals.

From puberty usually one mature egg is released every month from one ovary (ovulation) while the uterus lining thickens; the egg moves into the oviduct where a sperm may fuse with it to form a zygote, which divides by mitosis while travelling to the uterus and implants in the thick lining — implantation marks the beginning of pregnancy.

If an egg is not fertilised it lives about a day and degenerates; the thick, blood-rich uterine lining is no longer needed and is shed with some blood through the vagina — menstruation (3–7 days); ovulation, preparation of the uterus and menstruation repeat every 21–35 days (often about 28) from puberty (10–14 years) to menopause (about 50).
Period is your pride: menstruation is a sign of a healthy reproductive system, not something to be ashamed of.
During pregnancy the menstrual cycle stops: the thick lining is needed to nourish the developing embryo, so it is not shed.

Human pregnancy lasts about nine months in three trimesters; the embryo forms major organs in the first two months and from about the ninth week is called a foetus; the uterus protects and nourishes it; at birth uterine muscles contract to push the baby out; the newborn needs breast milk, warmth and vaccines, and the mother needs good food, check-ups, rest and emotional support.
Childbirth: strong contractions of the uterine muscles push the foetus out through the birth canal; if a normal birth is not safe, doctors use medical or surgical procedures.
Post-partum depression (anxiety and fatigue after delivery) is a recognised, treatable condition — mothers should talk to a doctor, nurse or ASHA worker.

notes.h: Reproductive Health: Maturity, STIs and Contraception
items: In adolescence the body becomes capable of reproduction gradually, but emotional maturity takes longer; responsible choices prevent unplanned pregnancies and sexually transmitted infections (STIs); condoms prevent both; other contraceptives (pills, IUDs, surgery) prevent pregnancy only; prenatal sex determination is banned in India to protect the sex ratio.
Wrong: An organism needs to reproduce to stay alive itself. Right: An individual can live without reproducing; reproduction is needed for its KIND (species) to continue after it dies
Wrong: Every new plant grows from a seed. Right: Potato, ginger, sugarcane and Bryophyllum make new plants from stems or leaves — no seed
Wrong: A grafted branch gives flowers that are a mix of Plant A and Plant B. Right: (added) The grafted stem of Plant B keeps its own variety — the yellow rose stays yellow; Plant A only gives roots
Wrong: Budding happens only in plants (flower buds). Right: Here a 'bud' is an outgrowth on yeast or hydra that becomes a new individual — not a flower bud
Wrong: Mould comes from the bread itself. Right: It grows from spores already present in the air (life only from pre-existing life — Pasteur)
Wrong: Asexual offspring are slightly different, like brothers and sisters. Right: Mitosis gives each daughter cell the same chromosomes, so they are identical clones

sol_items: Anthers removed, pollen from another plant dusted, seed...: Cross-pollination.
Order: pollen germination, fertilisation, pollination, ...: Pollination → pollen germination → fertilisation → zygote formation.
Why are asexual offspring genetically identical to the ...: They arise from one parent by cell division with no mixing of genes.
Why does the menstrual cycle stop during pregnancy: Hormones keep the uterus lining in place and stop ovulation.
Why are night-blooming flowers white or light colo: They are visible in the dark and attract night pollinators.
Why are vegetatively propagated plants more vulnerable ...: They are genetically identical, so one disease can spread to all.

A single parent produces offspring that are almost exact copies of the parent.

items: Biodiversity is the immense variety of living organisms. Every organism has a role in keeping nature stable, humans depend on it, and India's varied landscapes hold many endemic species and parts of four global hotspots.
Biodiversity = variety of life.
Endemic = found only in one region.
Hotspot = many endemic species + much habitat lost.

notes.h: How and Why We Classify Organisms
items: The same organism can be grouped in many ways, so scientists use agreed criteria — from easily visible features to cells and DNA. This biological classification makes the vast diversity easy to study, compare, name and conserve.
Broad visible features first, detailed features later.
Similar features suggest common ancestors.

Classification grew with knowledge: Aristotle used habitat; then two, three, four and finally Whittaker's five kingdoms as microscopes revealed nuclei and fungi were understood; DNA studies later gave three domains.
Whittaker's five kingdoms are separated by four questions: prokaryote or eukaryote? unicellular or multicellular? cell wall (and of what)? autotrophic or heterotrophic?

Monera are single-celled prokaryotes — bacteria and cyanobacteria — with no true nucleus. They live everywhere; some cause disease, many are useful, and cyanobacteria make food and gave the Earth its early oxygen.

Protista are single-celled eukaryotes — Amoeba, Paramecium, Euglena — with a true nucleus and no cell wall or a cellulose wall; they live in water and moist places, and one cell carries out every life process.
Fungi are mostly multicellular eukaryotes with chitin cell walls that cannot make food; they absorb it, mostly from dead matter, so they are the great decomposers.
Fungi: chitin wall + absorb food.
Most are saprophytes; some mutualistic, some parasitic.
Reproduce sexually and asexually, often by spores; grow best warm and moist.

notes.h: Plants Without Seeds — Thallophyta, Bryophyta and Pteridophyta
items: Plants are multicellular autotrophs with cellulose walls. The first three classes show the move from water to land: Thallophyta live in water, Bryophyta reach moist land, Pteridophyta gain xylem and phloem — but all three still need water to reproduce and make no seeds.
Bryophytes = 'amphibians' of the plant kingdom.
Taller plants need xylem and phloem because water and food must travel far.

Gymnosperms and angiosperms reproduce without water and make seeds that protect the embryo with stored food; gymnosperm seeds are naked on cones, angiosperm seeds are inside fruits, and flowers make angiosperms the most diverse plants.
Seed = protected embryo + stored food.
Gymnosperms: cold, dry regions. Angiosperms: widest range of environments.

notes.h: Kingdom Animalia and the Simple Invertebrates
items: Animals are multicellular heterotrophs, split by the notochord into non-chordates and chordates. From sponges to earthworms each phylum adds a body feature: tissues, bilateral symmetry, a second opening, segments and a body cavity.

Arthropods add jointed legs and a hard outer skeleton, molluscs protect soft bodies with shells, echinoderms gain an inner skeleton without a notochord; then chordates appear — protochordates with a notochord, vertebrates with a backbone.
Looking across invertebrates: complexity increases; each new feature improves feeding, movement or protection but brings new challenges.
Notochord → backbone in vertebrates.
Classification is a ladder of ranks from kingdom to species; every lower group is part of the one above, and lower ranks have fewer members sharing more features — like an address.
Every organism has one two-part scientific name — genus (capital) + species (small), in italics or underlined — used worldwide instead of many local names.

Small differences that helped survival and reproduction piled up over many generations, giving new forms; body structures like fins, feathers and fur are outcomes of such change, and fossils in rock layers are the evidence.
Generally, older rock layers hold simpler organisms and newer layers more complex ones.
Diversity = outcome of continuous change over a vast span of time.
Every species has a role; pollution, deforestation, overuse of resources and climate change are reducing biodiversity, and the loss of one species can pull down others that depend on it.
Wrong: Biodiversity means only the number of animals in a place. Right: It is the variety of ALL life — microbes, fungi, plants, animals — and the varied habitats and crop varieties too
Wrong: Each organism belongs to only one group. Right: It depends on the criterion: by eating habit an owl is a carnivore, by activity time it is nocturnal
Wrong: Old systems like Aristotle's were simply wrong. Right: Each system fitted the knowledge and tools of its time; it changed when new evidence came
Wrong: Fungi and plants are one kingdom because both have cell walls. Right: Fungi walls are chitin and fungi cannot make food; plant walls are cellulose and plants photosynthesise
Wrong: All bacteria are harmful germs. Right: Some are pathogens, but many are useful — Lactobacillus, Rhizobium, biogas and pollutant-eating bacteria
Wrong: Every single-celled organism is a bacterium. Right: Single cells WITH a true nucleus (Amoeba, Euglena) are protists, not Monera

Which feature of sponge cells supports placing them in ...: They have no cell wall and are heterotrophic.
Why is cellular organisation more fundamental than xyle...: All living things are made of cells, so it is the basic way to classify.
Unlabelled slide: single cell, well-defined nucleus, ma...: Kingdom Protista (e.g., Paramecium).
How does diversity help an ecosystem?: Many species keep food webs and nutrient cycles stable.
Why are viruses not placed in any of the five king: They are non-cellular and show life only inside a host.

notes.h: Earth's Spheres and How They Interact
items: The Earth is one system of five spheres — geosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, atmosphere and biosphere — and a disturbance in one sphere leads to changes in the others.
Five spheres: geo (rock), hydro (liquid water), cryo (ice), atmo (air), bio (life)
The Sun is the main energy source; the Earth's hot interior and chemical reactions also drive flows
A disturbance in one sphere spreads to the others

notes.h: Solar Radiation, Insolation and Solar Constant
items: The Sun's energy reaches the Earth as electromagnetic waves, mostly as UV, visible and infrared; the energy reaching the top of the atmosphere is the solar constant (≈ 1.4 kW m⁻²) and what reaches the surface is insolation (at most ≈ 1 kW m⁻²).
EM waves need no medium
~99% of solar energy: UV + visible + IR
Solar constant ≈ 1.4 kW m⁻² (top of atmosphere) > insolation ≈ 1 kW m⁻² (surface)
E = intensity × area × time

notes.h: Albedo: Why Some Surfaces Heat More
items: Albedo is the fraction of solar radiation a surface reflects: high-albedo surfaces (snow, ice) reflect more and stay cool; low-albedo surfaces (black soil, ocean water, dark roads) absorb more and warm up.
Albedo = fraction reflected
Snow 0.80–0.90 → polar regions cold
Low albedo (black soil, ocean) → warmer
Re-radiation keeps cities warm at night — urban heat island

notes.h: Latitude and Earth's Shape: Why the Equator Is Hotter
items: Because the Earth is a sphere, the Sun's rays strike different latitudes at different angles: at the equator the energy is concentrated on a small area, at the poles it is spread over a large area — so the equator stays warm and the poles cold.
Same sunlight, different angles
Equator: concentrated → warm; poles: spread → cold
Shape + tilt + revolution → seasons and changing day length
Equator–pole temperature difference drives global winds and ocean currents

notes.h: Role of the Atmosphere: Layers, Ozone and Greenhouse Effect
items: The atmosphere (mainly N₂ 78%, O₂ 21%) is layered: weather happens in the troposphere, heated from the surface; ozone in the stratosphere absorbs UV. It protects life in two ways — it absorbs part of the incoming radiation and traps outgoing heat (greenhouse effect).
Troposphere 0–12 km: weather, cools with height
Stratosphere 12–50 km: ozone, warms with height
Two roles: absorb incoming UV; trap outgoing IR

notes.h: Valley Breeze and Mountain Breeze (Local Winds)
items: Mountain slopes and valley floors heat and cool at different rates: by day warm air rises from sun-heated slopes and cool valley air moves up (valley breeze); at night cool dense air flows down the slopes into the valley (mountain breeze).
Day: slopes warm → valley breeze up
Night: slopes cool → mountain breeze down
Same idea as land and sea breezes, on hills

Uneven heating between the equator and the poles creates alternating low and high pressure belts (0°, 30°, 60°, 90°); air moving between them forms planetary winds, which the Earth's rotation deflects into curved paths.
Rising air → low pressure; sinking air → high pressure
Deflection: right in N, left in S

notes.h: Ocean Currents: How Oceans Carry Heat
items: Ocean currents are continuous movements of large masses of ocean water, driven by planetary winds and by differences in temperature and salinity, turned into gyres by the Earth's rotation; they carry heat from the equator toward the poles and transport nutrients.
Winds drag surface water
Cold or salty water sinks; warm or less salty water stays up
Gyres: clockwise N, counter-clockwise S
Currents move heat poleward and carry nutrients

Water evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation and returns to the ocean, carrying dissolved minerals and nutrients; climate change is making this cycle more extreme — heavier rain in some places, drought in others, and more run-off.
Evaporation → condensation → precipitation → run-off / infiltration
Water carries minerals and nutrients
Warmer air holds more moisture → extremes
Heavy bursts → run-off, erosion, less recharge

notes.h: Carbon Cycle: Fast Cycle, Slow Cycle and Ocean
items: Carbon, the backbone of life, circulates between the atmosphere, biosphere, geosphere and hydrosphere: a fast cycle (photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition) over days to years, a slow cycle (fossil fuels) over millions of years, and constant exchange with the ocean. Human activity has raised CO₂ from 315 to 420 ppm since 1960.
Carbon is the backbone of life
Fast cycle: photosynthesis ↔ respiration, decomposition
Slow cycle: fossil fuels; burning is fast
Ocean holds 71%, air ~1%

Nitrogen gas is the largest store of nitrogen but is non-reactive, so bacteria (and lightning, and the Haber-Bosch process) must convert it into compounds plants can absorb; the cycle runs through fixation, nitrification, assimilation, ammonification and denitrification.
N₂ is the largest store but non-reactive
Fixation → nitrification → assimilation → ammonification → denitrification
Bacteria do almost every step
Haber-Bosch: fertilisers; overuse harms soil and water

notes.h: Oxygen Cycle: Use and Restoration of Oxygen
items: Oxygen (21% of the atmosphere) is used in respiration and combustion, which release CO₂, and is restored by photosynthesis; this balance keeps the oxygen level of the air steady.
21% of air is O₂
Used: respiration, combustion, oxide formation
Restored: photosynthesis
Balance keeps O₂ steady

A biogeochemical cycle is the cyclic movement of matter and energy between the abiotic and biotic components of the Earth; the water, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen cycles keep nutrients available, sustain life, regulate climate and balance ecosystems.
Matter cycles between biotic and abiotic parts
Cycles keep nutrients available, sustain life, regulate climate, balance ecosystems
Cycles are linked to one another

Burning fossil fuels, deforestation and fertiliser overuse disrupt the carbon, nitrogen and water cycles across all spheres — warming, ocean acidification, eutrophication, smog — but global cooperation and local actions can restore the balance.
Excess CO₂ → warming and ocean acidification
Fertiliser overuse → eutrophication
Deforestation affects air, water, soil and life
Montreal worked; Kyoto and Paris less so
Wrong: Each sphere works on its own, separate from the others. Right: The spheres keep exchanging energy and matter, so a change in one changes the others
Wrong: Sunlight needs air to travel, like sound. Right: EM waves travel through the vacuum of space at 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; only sound needs a medium
Wrong: A surface with high albedo gets hotter. Right: High albedo means it REFLECTS more, so it stays cooler
Wrong: The equator is hotter because it is closer to the Sun. Right: It is the angle: rays at the equator fall on a smaller area, so energy is concentrated
Wrong: Sunlight heats the air directly from above, so higher air is warmer. Right: The surface absorbs sunlight and re-radiates IR; the troposphere is heated from below, so it gets colder with height
Wrong: Warm air sinks and cool air rises. Right: Warm air is less dense and rises; cool, dense air sinks

sol_items: Which atmospheric layer is responsible for weather: The troposphere, as it has most of the air, water vapour and clouds.
How does albedo affect temperature?: A high albedo (ice, snow) reflects light and cools; a low albedo (dark land) absorbs and warms.
Why is excess CO₂ undesirable though plants need i: Too much CO₂ traps heat and causes global warming.
Impacts of deforestation: Less photosynthesis, so less oxygen and more CO₂; soil erosion and loss of habitat.
Path of carbon back to the atmosphere: Plants → animals → respiration, decay, burning of fuels → CO₂ in the air.
Explain the nitrogen cycle: Bacteria fix nitrogen into nitrates for plants; animals eat plants; denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen to the air.
imp_items: Which sphere does a Himalayan glacier belong to, and which sphere does it feed?
Cryosphere; as it melts it feeds rivers in the hydrosphere.
Give one chain that shows a change in the atmosphere reaching the biosphere.
Warmer air → glaciers melt → sea level rises → coastal habitats are lost.
Why is the insolation at the surface less than the solar constant?
Gases, clouds and dust absorb and scatter part of the radiation on the way down.
Energy on 3 m² in 1 hour at 1 kW m⁻²?
Snow has albedo 0.85. What fraction of sunlight does it absorb?
Two equal beams of sunlight: one hits 1 m², the other spreads over 2 m². Which ground warms more?
The 1 m² — the same energy is concentrated on a smaller area.
